reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is a heterogeneous group of heritable connective-tissue disorders unified by joint hypermobility, skin hyperextensibility, and tissue fragility

The current international classification recognises multiple subtypes, most with an identified collagen or collagen-processing gene defect, though the common hypermobile type still lacks a confirmed molecular marker
Classical EDS is usually caused by variants in COL5A1 or COL5A2 and features marked skin hyperextensibility, atrophic scarring, and generalised joint hypermobility
Vascular EDS, caused by COL3A1 variants, is the most dangerous subtype because of spontaneous arterial, intestinal, and uterine rupture
The Beighton score is used to quantify generalised joint hypermobility as part of clinical assessment
Diagnosis combines clinical criteria for each subtype with targeted molecular genetic testing, which is especially important to confirm or exclude vascular EDS
Management is largely supportive, with physiotherapy, joint protection, skin and wound care, and pain management, plus vascular surveillance in the vascular type
In vascular EDS, medical measures to reduce arterial wall stress and avoidance of arterial catheterisation and elective vascular procedures are important
reference.pathophysiology: The Ehlers-Danlos syndromes result from defects in the synthesis, structure, or processing of collagen and related extracellular matrix components. Depending on the subtype, variants affect fibrillar collagens (such as type V in classical EDS and type III in vascular EDS) or enzymes and cofactors involved in collagen modification and cross-linking. Abnormal collagen fibrils reduce the tensile strength and integrity of skin, ligaments, blood vessels, and hollow organs, producing hypermobility, skin fragility with poor wound healing, and, in the most severe forms, catastrophic vascular and visceral rupture. The wide phenotypic range reflects which matrix component and tissue are predominantly affected.
additionalDifferentials: Generalised joint hypermobility without a defined syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Structured clinical assessment including the Beighton hypermobility score
Molecular genetic testing with a connective-tissue gene panel, prioritising COL3A1 when vascular EDS is suspected
Skin biopsy for collagen electron microscopy or biochemical study in selected cases
Echocardiography to assess for aortic root dilatation and mitral valve prolapse
Vascular imaging (CT or MR angiography) in suspected or confirmed vascular EDS
Bone assessment where osteogenesis imperfecta overlap is considered
redFlags: Sudden severe abdominal, chest, or flank pain suggesting arterial or visceral rupture in vascular EDS
Unexplained bruising with a family history of premature sudden death from vascular causes
Pregnancy in vascular EDS, given the risk of uterine and arterial rupture
Rapidly expanding haematoma or signs of internal haemorrhage
Recurrent large-joint dislocations causing severe disability
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends heavily on subtype: most patients with classical or hypermobile EDS have a normal lifespan with chronic musculoskeletal symptoms, whereas vascular EDS carries a substantially reduced life expectancy from arterial and organ rupture. Early recognition of the vascular subtype and appropriate precautions are the most important determinants of outcome.
pitfalls: Treating all EDS as benign and missing the life-threatening vascular subtype
Performing arterial catheterisation or elective vascular surgery in vascular EDS without weighing the high rupture risk
Assuming a normal molecular test excludes hypermobile EDS, which has no confirmed gene
Underestimating chronic pain, fatigue, and autonomic symptoms in affected patients
Neglecting genetic counselling and family screening, particularly for vascular EDS
references: The international classification of the Ehlers-Danlos syndromes
